course.title: Unity C# Scripting & Engine Architecture: Advanced Patterns, Systems & Production Code
course.description: An advanced deep-dive into Unity engine architecture for developers who have completed the beginner course. Covers event-driven architecture, ScriptableObject patterns, custom editors, the Job System, DOTS/ECS fundamentals, addressables, advanced optimization, and production-grade code architecture. By the end, you will architect scalable game systems, write editor tools, understand Unity's memory model, and build performance-critical code using modern Unity APIs.

blocks.value: Beyond MonoBehaviour: Clean Architecture
The beginner course taught component-based design. At the intermediate level, you separate concerns further — business logic should not live in MonoBehaviours that are coupled to Unity's lifecycle.
Core principles of clean Unity architecture:

items: **Single Responsibility** — Each class does one thing. A PlayerMovement class should not handle UI or audio.
**Dependency Inversion** — High-level modules depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete implementations.
**Composition over Inheritance** — Favor composing behaviors from smaller parts rather than deep inheritance chains.
**Separation of Concerns** — Split game logic, presentation, input, and data into distinct layers.

blocks.value: The Service Locator Pattern
Service Locator is a global registry of services. It is easy to implement but easy to abuse.

items: Easy to implement, easy to abuse
Hides dependencies — you cannot tell what a class needs by looking at its constructor
Hard to test — services are global state
Good for: small projects, rapid prototyping, truly global systems (Audio, Input)

blocks.output: Service Locator: global registry with hidden dependencies. Easy to set up but creates tight coupling to global state.

blocks.question: Why is Service Locator considered an anti-pattern in large projects?
options: It is too slow at runtime
It hides dependencies, making code hard to test and maintain
It requires too many interfaces
It only works with MonoBehaviours
blocks.correctAnswer: It hides dependencies, making code hard to test and maintain
blocks.explanation: Service Locator makes dependencies implicit. You cannot tell what a class needs by looking at its constructor. This makes unit testing impossible (you cannot mock dependencies) and maintenance difficult because changing one service can break classes you did not know used it.

blocks.value: Dependency Injection (DI)
Dependency Injection is the opposite of Service Locator. Dependencies are passed in explicitly, not found globally.

items: Dependencies are explicit — constructor tells you everything the class needs
Easy to mock for unit tests
More setup code, but pays off in large projects
Good for: complex systems, teams, long-term maintenance

blocks.output: Dependency Injection: explicit constructor parameters, factory wiring for MonoBehaviours, and pure C# classes with constructor injection.

blocks.value: DI Container: Manual Wiring
For larger projects, a simple DI container can automate wiring without external libraries like Zenject.

blocks.output: Simple DI Container with singleton registration, factory registration, and a GameBootstrapper that wires everything at startup.

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of Dependency Injection over Service Locator?
options: DI runs faster at runtime
DI makes dependencies explicit and testable
DI requires less code to set up
DI works without MonoBehaviours
blocks.correctAnswer: DI makes dependencies explicit and testable
blocks.explanation: The key advantage of DI is that dependencies are visible in constructors. This makes it obvious what a class needs, enables easy mocking in unit tests, and prevents hidden coupling to global state. Service Locator hides these dependencies.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Event Bus Pattern — Decoupled Communication

blocks.value: Event Bus Pattern: Decoupled Communication
Direct references between objects create tight coupling. The Event Bus lets objects communicate without knowing about each other.
When to use Event Bus vs direct references:

items: Use **direct references** for parent-child relationships and tightly coupled systems (Player → PlayerHealth)
Use **Event Bus** for cross-cutting concerns (EnemyDied → UI updates, score, achievements, spawn manager)
Use **C# events** on components for local notifications within a subsystem
Use **UnityEvents** (Inspector-configurable) for designer-friendly hooks

blocks.output: Type-safe generic Event Bus with struct events and a publisher that knows nothing about subscribers.

blocks.value: Subscribers: Completely Decoupled

blocks.output: Multiple decoupled subscribers (ScoreManager, AchievementTracker, SpawnManager) responding to the same event without knowing about each other.

blocks.question: Your game has 15 different systems that need to respond when a player completes a level (UI, achievements, analytics, save system, next level unlock). What is the best architecture?
options: Have the LevelManager hold direct references to all 15 systems and call their methods
Use an Event Bus where LevelManager publishes a LevelCompletedEvent and each system subscribes independently
Use a giant switch statement in LevelManager
Have each system poll LevelManager every frame to check if the level is done
blocks.correctAnswer: Use an Event Bus where LevelManager publishes a LevelCompletedEvent and each system subscribes independently
blocks.explanation: Direct references create a maintenance nightmare — add a 16th system and you must modify LevelManager. A switch statement is unmaintainable. Polling wastes CPU. The Event Bus decouples the publisher from subscribers: LevelManager knows nothing about who listens, and new systems can subscribe without touching existing code. This is the core of event-driven architecture.

parts.partTitle: Part 4: State Machines for Complex Behaviors

blocks.value: State Machines for Complex Behaviors
Boolean flags (isAttacking, isStunned, isDead) quickly become unmanageable. A proper state machine enforces valid transitions and encapsulates state-specific logic.
Benefits of state machines:

items: Only valid state transitions are allowed — no accidental 'dead but attacking' bugs
Each state is self-contained — enter, update, exit logic is isolated
Easy to debug — you can log every state transition
Scalable — adding new states does not touch existing ones

blocks.output: Generic StateMachine<T> and State<T> base classes with typed state transitions and lifecycle hooks.

blocks.value: Enemy AI State Machine Implementation

blocks.output: Complete Enemy AI with 6 states, valid transitions, encapsulated per-state logic, and global health check that overrides any state.

blocks.question: What is the primary benefit of using a State Machine over boolean flags for AI behavior?
options: State machines use less memory
State machines enforce valid transitions and prevent impossible state combinations
State machines are easier to serialize to JSON
State machines require less code
blocks.correctAnswer: State machines enforce valid transitions and prevent impossible state combinations
blocks.explanation: Boolean flags allow any combination (e.g., isAttacking AND isDead simultaneously). A state machine enforces that only one state is active at a time and that transitions follow defined rules. This eliminates an entire class of bugs where objects are in logically impossible states.

blocks.value: ScriptableObjects as Game Data

ScriptableObjects are data containers that live in your project, not in scenes. They are the foundation of data-driven design — separating 'what can exist' (data) from 'what currently exists' (runtime instances).
Key advantages over MonoBehaviour data:

items: Shared across scenes — no duplication, no sync issues
Designer-friendly — non-programmers can balance stats via Inspector
Version control friendly — changes are in asset files, not scene files
Cannot be modified at runtime in builds (immutable reference data)
Instantiate with CreateInstance<T>() for runtime-modifiable copies

blocks.output: WeaponData ScriptableObject with identity, combat stats, recoil curves, spread mechanics, audio/visual references, and rarity/economy data.

blocks.value: Enemy Data & Loot Tables

blocks.output: EnemyData with AI behavior and scaling, LootTable with weighted random drops, and ItemData for inventory management.

blocks.question: Why are ScriptableObjects better than storing data in MonoBehaviour components for game balancing?
options: ScriptableObjects run faster at runtime
ScriptableObjects are shared assets editable outside scenes, making version control and balancing easier
ScriptableObjects can only be created by programmers
ScriptableObjects automatically sync data between all scenes
blocks.correctAnswer: ScriptableObjects are shared assets editable outside scenes, making version control and balancing easier
blocks.explanation: ScriptableObjects live as asset files, not in scene files. This means designers can tweak values without opening scenes, changes are tracked in version control as small diffs (not massive scene file changes), and the same data asset can be referenced across multiple scenes without duplication.

blocks.value: ScriptableObject Runtime Instances

ScriptableObject assets are shared and immutable in builds. But you can create runtime instances that are independent copies — perfect for weapon upgrades, modified enemy stats, or player inventory items.

blocks.output: Runtime WeaponInstance with mutable stats, spread recovery, recoil curves, and upgrade system.

blocks.value: Inventory System Using Runtime Instances

blocks.output: Inventory managing multiple WeaponInstance objects with equip and upgrade functionality.

blocks.question: Why create runtime instances of ScriptableObjects instead of modifying the asset directly?
options: Runtime instances are faster to create
ScriptableObject assets are shared and immutable in builds; runtime instances allow per-object state
ScriptableObjects cannot be modified at all
Runtime instances use less memory
blocks.correctAnswer: ScriptableObject assets are shared and immutable in builds; runtime instances allow per-object state
blocks.explanation: ScriptableObject assets are shared references. Modifying one would affect all users of that asset. Runtime instances (created via new Class() or CreateInstance) are independent copies that can hold per-object mutable state like current ammo, upgrade level, and durability.

blocks.value: ScriptableObject Singletons (Game Architecture)
ScriptableObjects can act as persistent, scene-independent singletons. They survive scene loads and do not require GameObjects.
This pattern is called ScriptableObject Architecture or Game Architecture with ScriptableObjects:

items: Create a GameStateSO asset that holds global game state (score, level, currency)
Create RuntimeSet<T> assets that track active objects (all enemies, all pickups)
Create GameEventSO assets for designer-configurable events
Reference these assets in any script via Inspector — no FindObjectOfType needed

blocks.output: Abstract RuntimeSet<T> with add/remove/getRandom/getNearest, plus concrete EnemyRuntimeSet and PlayerRuntimeSet.

blocks.value: GameEventSO: Designer-Friendly Events

blocks.output: ScriptableObject architecture: RuntimeSet for tracking active enemies, GameEventSO for designer-friendly events, and automatic registration/unregistration.

blocks.question: You need to track all active enemies in the scene for a spawn manager, minimap, and AI director. What is the most robust approach?
options: Use FindObjectsOfType<EnemyAI>() in each system every few seconds
Use a ScriptableObject RuntimeSet that enemies register/unregister via OnEnable/OnDisable
Have the SpawnManager maintain a static List<EnemyAI> that other systems access
Use SendMessage("RegisterEnemy") on all GameObjects when an enemy spawns
blocks.correctAnswer: Use a ScriptableObject RuntimeSet that enemies register/unregister via OnEnable/OnDisable
blocks.explanation: FindObjectsOfType is slow and misses dynamically spawned/destroyed enemies. A static list creates hidden coupling and lifecycle bugs. SendMessage is slow, string-based, and deprecated. The RuntimeSet pattern: enemies self-register on enable, self-remove on disable. The asset is shared via Inspector references — no searching, no static state, works across scenes, and is designer-friendly.

blocks.value: Custom Property Drawers
Property drawers customize how fields appear in the Inspector. They make complex data types editable and validate input automatically.
Common use cases:

items: Draw a struct with multiple fields as a single compact line
Add buttons directly in the Inspector for quick actions
Show/hide fields based on other field values
Validate input and show error messages in real-time
Draw custom graphs, curves, or visualizations for data

blocks.output: Custom PropertyDrawer for MinMaxFloat struct: compact two-field line with built-in validation highlighting when min exceeds max.

blocks.value: Range Slider Property Drawer

blocks.output: RangedFloat PropertyDrawer with a slider showing current value between min and max, plus editable min/max fields.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of a CustomPropertyDrawer in Unity?
options: To replace the entire Inspector for a MonoBehaviour
To customize how a specific field type is drawn in the Inspector
To create standalone editor windows
To modify the Unity engine source code
blocks.correctAnswer: To customize how a specific field type is drawn in the Inspector
blocks.explanation: PropertyDrawers customize the visual representation of a specific field type (like a struct or class) wherever it appears in the Inspector. They are reusable across any MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject that uses that type. Custom Editors replace the entire Inspector for one class. EditorWindows are standalone tools.

blocks.value: Custom Inspector Editors
Custom Editors completely replace the default Inspector for a MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject. They give you full control over the editing experience.

blocks.output: Custom Editor with styled headers, ScriptableObject preview, quick action buttons, debug foldout, and automatic scene dirty marking.

blocks.value: Multi-Object Editing Support

blocks.output: Custom Editor with multi-object editing, help boxes, scene view gizmos for visualizing spawn radius.

blocks.question: What is the difference between a PropertyDrawer and a Custom Editor?
options: PropertyDrawers are faster than Custom Editors
PropertyDrawers customize a field type everywhere; Custom Editors replace the entire Inspector for one class
PropertyDrawers only work with structs; Custom Editors only work with classes
There is no difference
blocks.correctAnswer: PropertyDrawers customize a field type everywhere; Custom Editors replace the entire Inspector for one class
blocks.explanation: PropertyDrawers are attached to types (structs/classes) and apply wherever that type is used as a field. Custom Editors are attached to specific MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject classes and replace their entire Inspector view. They serve different purposes and can be used together.

parts.partTitle: Part 10: Custom Attributes for Validation & Workflow

blocks.value: Custom Attributes for Validation & Workflow
Attributes are C# metadata that Unity reads to modify behavior. You can create custom attributes and property drawers to enforce team conventions and speed up workflow.

blocks.output: Three custom attributes with property drawers: Min for value clamping, SceneName for dropdown selection, ReadOnlyInPlayMode for design-time protection.

blocks.value: Usage Example

blocks.output: GameConfig using all three custom attributes, plus a bonus Tag attribute with TagField drawer.

blocks.question: You want to create a custom dropdown in the Inspector that shows all scene names from Build Settings. Which approach is correct?
options: Create a custom Editor class and override OnInspectorGUI for every MonoBehaviour that needs it
Create a [SceneName] PropertyAttribute and a CustomPropertyDrawer that reads EditorBuildSettings.scenes
Use a string field and validate it in OnValidate() with a warning message
Create a custom EditorWindow that lists scenes and copies the name to clipboard
blocks.correctAnswer: Create a [SceneName] PropertyAttribute and a CustomPropertyDrawer that reads EditorBuildSettings.scenes
blocks.explanation: PropertyAttributes with PropertyDrawers are reusable across any field in any class. You write the drawer once, and any field marked with [SceneName] gets the dropdown automatically. Custom Editors require writing a new class for every MonoBehaviour. OnValidate only runs at runtime. EditorWindows are not integrated into the Inspector workflow.

blocks.value: Editor Windows for Level Design Tools
Editor Windows are standalone tools inside Unity. They are perfect for batch operations, level design helpers, and data management that would be tedious in the Inspector.

blocks.question: What is the key advantage of an EditorWindow over a Custom Inspector?
options: EditorWindows are faster to render
EditorWindows are standalone tools that can operate on multiple objects and perform batch operations

blocks.correctAnswer: EditorWindows are standalone tools that can operate on multiple objects and perform batch operations
blocks.explanation: EditorWindows are independent panels that can perform operations across the entire project or selection, not just one object. They are ideal for batch operations, level design tools, and data management that would be tedious in per-object Inspectors.

blocks.value: Why Unity's Job System Matters

Unity's main thread handles rendering, input, and script execution. Heavy computation on the main thread causes frame drops. The Job System lets you write multithreaded code that runs safely on worker threads while integrating cleanly with Unity's engine loop.
Key concepts:

items: Jobs are structs that implement IJob or IJobParallelFor — they contain data and an Execute method
Job structs must be blittable (no managed types like classes, strings, or MonoBehaviours)
JobHandles track dependencies — jobs automatically wait for prerequisite jobs to complete
Burst Compiler compiles jobs to highly optimized native code using LLVM
NativeArray<T> is the primary data container — it is unmanaged memory that jobs can read/write

blocks.output: IJobParallelFor moves 10,000 objects across worker threads using NativeArrays, with proper memory disposal in OnDestroy.

blocks.value: NativeArray Memory Management

blocks.output: NativeArray allocator types and disposal patterns for safe memory management in the Job System.

blocks.question: What must a job struct contain to be compatible with the Job System?
options: It must inherit from MonoBehaviour
It must be a struct with only blittable types (no classes, strings, or MonoBehaviours)
It must use the [BurstCompile] attribute
It must implement IDisposable
blocks.correctAnswer: It must be a struct with only blittable types (no classes, strings, or MonoBehaviours)
blocks.explanation: Job structs must be blittable because they are copied to worker thread memory. Managed types like classes, strings, and MonoBehaviours cannot be used. The [BurstCompile] attribute is optional but recommended for performance. IDisposable is not required.

blocks.value: Job Dependencies & Chaining
Jobs can depend on other jobs. Unity's JobHandle system ensures jobs execute in the correct order without manual synchronization primitives like locks or mutexes.

blocks.output: Two-job dependency chain: parallel distance calculation followed by single-threaded minimum finding, with automatic synchronization via JobHandle passing.

blocks.value: Three-Job Pipeline: Sort then Process

blocks.output: Three-job pipeline: calculate distances, sort results, then process top N — each job depends on the previous via JobHandle.

blocks.question: How do you ensure Job B runs only after Job A completes?
options: Use a lock/mutex between the jobs
Pass Job A's JobHandle to Job B's Schedule method
Call Complete() on Job A before scheduling Job B
Use a Coroutine to wait between them
blocks.correctAnswer: Pass Job A's JobHandle to Job B's Schedule method
blocks.explanation: The Job System handles synchronization automatically. Pass the dependency JobHandle as the third parameter to Schedule() or ScheduleParallel(). Unity ensures the dependent job waits for its prerequisites. Calling Complete() blocks the main thread, which defeats the purpose of parallelism.

blocks.value: ECS (Entity Component System) Fundamentals
ECS is Unity's data-oriented architecture. Instead of MonoBehaviours on GameObjects, you have Entities (IDs), Components (pure data structs), and Systems (logic that processes component data).
ECS advantages over OOP MonoBehaviour:

items: Cache-friendly memory layout — components stored in contiguous arrays, not scattered across heap
No virtual method overhead — systems process data in tight loops
Automatic multithreading — systems run in parallel where dependencies allow
Burst compilation — C# jobs compile to SIMD-optimized native code
Scales to 100,000+ entities — MonoBehaviour overhead becomes prohibitive

blocks.output: Complete ECS setup: IComponentData structs, ISystem with entity queries, EntityManager spawning 10,000 entities with RenderMeshArray.

blocks.value: Burst-Compiled IJobEntity

blocks.output: Burst-compiled IJobEntity for parallel rotation processing, plus baked entity instantiation from prefabs.

blocks.question: In ECS, what does an Entity represent?
options: A MonoBehaviour with attached components
A lightweight ID that groups components together
A GameObject in the scene hierarchy
A C# class that inherits from Component
blocks.correctAnswer: A lightweight ID that groups components together
blocks.explanation: In ECS, an Entity is just an integer ID. It has no data and no behavior of its own. Components (structs implementing IComponentData) hold the data, and Systems process entities that have specific combinations of components. This is fundamentally different from MonoBehaviour where the object IS the behavior.

blocks.value: Burst Compiler & Mathematics Library
The Burst Compiler transforms IL code into highly optimized native machine code. Combined with Unity.Mathematics, you get SIMD vectorization and cache-friendly operations.

blocks.output: BurstCompile attribute, Unity.Mathematics float3 types, spatial hashing with prime-based hashing, and SIMD-optimized vector normalization.

blocks.value: Unity.Mathematics Cheat Sheet

blocks.output: Unity.Mathematics replacements and Burst-optimized physics simulation with branchless conditional using math.select().

blocks.question: You have 50,000 projectiles that need their positions updated every frame with collision checks. Which approach gives the best performance?
options: MonoBehaviour Update() on each projectile with GetComponent calls
Single MonoBehaviour with a List<Projectile> and foreach loop in Update()
IJobParallelFor with NativeArrays, BurstCompile, and Unity.Mathematics
Coroutine on each projectile with yield return null
blocks.correctAnswer: IJobParallelFor with NativeArrays, BurstCompile, and Unity.Mathematics
blocks.explanation: MonoBehaviour Update() has massive overhead per object (virtual calls, cache misses). A List<Projectile> in a single MonoBehaviour is better but still single-threaded. Coroutines have even more overhead than Update(). IJobParallelFor distributes work across CPU cores, NativeArrays provide cache-friendly contiguous memory, BurstCompile generates SIMD-optimized machine code, and Unity.Mathematics replaces heavy Vector3 operations with lightweight float3 structs. This combination can process 50,000 entities 50-100x faster than MonoBehaviour approaches.
